title: Sense amp fused with time-to-digital converter as retention canary
idea: Combine every sense-amp stripe with a shared 6-bit time-to-digital converter that timestamps how long each bitline pair takes to cross the latch threshold during ordinary activations; slow-resolving (low-charge) rows are logged in a small per-bank table and refreshed at 64 ms while all others drop to 256-1024 ms. Normal reads become free, continuous retention measurements, which also catches variable-retention cells that offline profiling misses.
why: Refresh (fact 3: 16-33% idle power, 10-20% bandwidth); in-field margin tracking could cut refresh operations ~4x.

title: Sub-wordline driver doubles as row-wise back-gate bias generator
idea: Build access transistors with a buried back gate patterned per row, and merge the back-gate driver into the existing sub-wordline driver: idle rows sit at about -1 V back bias to choke the leakage tail, and the activated row flips to forward bias for stronger drive. One driver serves two gates, so no extra decoder is needed.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): a 150-200 mV effective Vt shift on idle rows could cut tail leakage ~10x (refresh 64 to ~512 ms); forward bias on the open row allows lower wordline voltage (fact 10).

title: Bitline as LC resonator read by frequency-division multiplexing
idea: Make each segmented bitline part of an LC tank (top-metal spiral over the array plus bitline capacitance) with its own resonant frequency; the cell charge shifts a varactor-loaded resonance, and one wideband RF receiver per mat reads 16 bitlines at once by FDM, replacing 16 pitch-matched latch sense amps. This combines RF filter-bank receivers with DRAM sensing.
why: Periphery ~49% (fact 7): one shared receiver per 16 bitlines; ~20-30% die-area savings if inductors fold over the array.

title: Wavelength-addressed wordline decoding with silicon microring filters
idea: Broadcast the row address as a WDM optical comb on a waveguide running over each bank; each sub-wordline driver group has a microring tuned to one wavelength plus a photodiode that fires its driver. The predecoder tree and its long, repeated global wires disappear, because a photonic add-drop filter now does the row decoder's job.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and data movement (fact 5): removes global decode wiring; ~30% lower decode energy and area in large banks, with optical I/O as a natural extension.

title: Shared oxide preamp in capacitor layer per eight cells
idea: Place one vertical IGZO or poly-Si source-follower in the BEOL capacitor layer for every 8 stacked-capacitor cells: the selected cell dumps charge onto a ~1 fF local node instead of a 60-80 fF bitline, and the preamp drives the long bitline. This combines plain 1T1C storage with gain-cell-style amplification at the cell-group level, not per cell.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): ~10x better transfer ratio lets Cs fall from 5 fF to ~1 fF and capacitor aspect ratio from ~70:1 to ~15:1, a large etch and capex relief.

title: Pulsed segmented cell plate borrowed from FeRAM boosts signal
idea: Split DRAM's common VDD/2 plate into row-wise segments and pulse the selected row's plate by +0.5 V during charge sharing (the FeRAM plate-line drive), so the stored node is coupled upward and the differential bitline signal grows; the plate returns to VDD/2 before restore.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and voltage floor (fact 10): ~1.5-2x bitline signal at the same Cs, allowing 30-40% lower Cs or longer bitlines (fewer SA stripes, fact 7).

title: Local wordline decoders with embedded antifuse tags for repair
idea: Give every local row decoder a tiny antifuse-programmed address-tag comparator, so any spare row in a mat answers for a failed address directly; the central fuse bank, fuse-broadcast bus and redundancy-compare stage are deleted, because the decoder and the repair CAM are now one cell.
why: Periphery (fact 7): repair logic and fuses are ~3-5% of die; also removes ~1 ns of compare from tRCD and allows finer, higher-yield repair.

title: Image-sensor floating-diffusion readout with correlated double sampling
idea: Adopt CMOS image-sensor pixel readout: a transfer gate moves cell charge onto a ~0.5 fF floating diffusion read by a source follower, sampled before and after transfer (correlated double sampling) to cancel kTC noise and offset at ~2 electrons rms. A cell then needs only ~1,000 electrons (~0.15 fF at 1 V).
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): Cs ~30x smaller, removing high-AR capacitor etch; the cost is a slower ~30-50 ns read, acceptable for a capacity tier.

title: HBM base die absorbs all core-die periphery
idea: Make HBM core dies array-only (cells plus wordline straps), hybrid-bond each one face-to-face to a logic-process periphery tier holding the SAs and decoders, and merge the base-die functions into the same periphery design, so the duplicate IO and TSV drivers on each core die disappear.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and HBM TSV tax (fact 6): array efficiency ~50% to ~85% (~1.6x bits per array wafer), with lower-power logic-process SAs.

title: Sense amp with nonvolatile ferroelectric offset trim
idea: Integrate a tiny HZO ferroelectric capacitor in each sense amp and program its polarization at wafer test so it couples a compensating charge onto the weak side of the latch, permanently trimming offset from ~15 mV to ~3 mV with no runtime calibration.
why: Sense margin (facts 1, 7): lower offset allows ~40% smaller SA devices, or ~2x longer bitlines (half the SA stripes), or smaller Cs.

title: Bucket-brigade row buffer replaces column decoder and datalines
idea: Turn the sensed row into a CCD-style charge-transfer shift register: after sensing, bits march out of the stripe edge in parallel lanes at GHz rates straight into the serializer, so the column decoder, column-select lines and global I/O sense amps are gone. This combines CCD readout with the DRAM row buffer.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and overfetch (fact 8): the column path is ~10% of die; streaming full rows turns the 128x overfetch into useful data for AI/streaming, ~3-5x lower pJ per useful bit.

title: Gate-on-array shift register walks refresh through wordline strips
idea: Borrow the LCD gate-driver-on-array (GOA) shift register: a ring of two-transistor shift stages embedded in each sub-wordline driver strip passes a refresh token row to row, so refresh activates rows without powering the refresh address counter, the predecoders or the global row bus.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): strips decode and global-wire energy (~30-40% of per-refresh energy) out of every refresh, sharply lowering self-refresh power.

title: Per-stripe adaptive array voltage regulated by sensed margin
idea: Put a micro-LDO in every SA stripe and close the loop with a replica sense pair on a programmable reference: the regulator lowers that subarray's VARY until measured margin reaches target, so strong subarrays run near 0.7 V while weak ones stay at 1.0 V.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): ~20% average VARY drop gives ~35% lower array CV^2 energy, with per-region guardbands instead of one worst-case guardband per die.

title: Negative-capacitance ferroelectric film as bitline signal amplifier
idea: Insert a thin doped-HfO2 negative-capacitance layer in series at the SA input gate (or at the bitline contact), capacitance-matched so the charge-sharing step has voltage gain above 1 and amplifies the cell signal before the latch fires.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): 2-3x signal gain would let Cs drop to ~2 fF and permit lower VARY (fact 10).

title: NEMS relay latch inside the sub-wordline driver
idea: Replace the sub-wordline driver's level shifter and pull-down with a nanoelectromechanical relay whose mechanical hysteresis both latches the wordline state and gives true zero off-leakage; low-voltage decode pulls it in and it switches the 3 V VPP line directly.
why: Voltage floor and periphery leakage (facts 10, 7): removes level-shifter area and the SWD leakage that dominates standby, and gives a perfectly held negative wordline on idle rows.

title: Resonant LC tank drives wordlines adiabatically, recycling boost energy
idea: Fuse resonant-clock-mesh design with wordline drive: wordlines in a bank charge from a sinusoidal resonant VPP rail set by an on-package inductor, so energy swings between the inductor and the wordline capacitance instead of being dumped to ground at every precharge.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): recovers ~60-70% of ~3 V wordline CV^2 energy, ~20-25% lower activation energy.

title: Liquid-nitrogen racks with cryo-CMOS periphery and no refresh
idea: Combine datacenter immersion-cooling infrastructure with 77 K operation: access-transistor leakage drops by orders of magnitude so retention reaches hours, and periphery gains ~2x mobility with lower wire resistance; redesign the periphery for 77 K with higher Vt and VDD near 0.6 V.
why: Refresh (fact 3) essentially eliminated and voltage floor (fact 10) relaxed; system energy per bit perhaps ~3x lower even after ~10 W/W cryocooler overhead.

title: Single-electron transistor electrometer senses attofarad cells
idea: Borrow spin-qubit readout: couple a silicon single-electron transistor capacitively to each micro-cell storage node and read it by RF reflectometry with frequency multiplexing, so cells storing only ~100 electrons can be read.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): Cs ~50x smaller (~0.02 fF), allowing planar cells and many cheap 3D tiers (fact 2); needs room-temperature SET operation, which is very hard.

title: Tunnel-FET input pair inside a conventional MOSFET latch
idea: Replace only the input pair of the DRAM sense amp with steep-slope tunnel FETs (sub-60 mV/decade) and keep MOSFETs for restore, so the latch begins amplifying at VARY ~0.5 V, where MOSFET-only latches barely turn on.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): halving VARY cuts bitline CV^2 energy ~4x, and refresh energy falls with it.

title: Oxide-TFT predecoders and test logic built over the array
idea: Move slow, low-drive periphery (row predecoders, fuse latches, test-mode logic, mode registers) into BEOL IGZO thin-film transistor layers built over the cell array, leaving only the sense amps and fast IO in silicon.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7): moving ~15-20% of die area into the space over the array gives ~1.2x bits per wafer without wafer bonding.

title: Tier-select transistor at each staircase step for 3D DRAM
idea: In stacked 3D DRAM, put a vertical oxide transistor at each staircase landing that acts as a tier decoder switch, so a few shared vertical wordline drivers fan out to N tiers through local selects; staircase contacts drop from N x rows to rows + N.
why: No manufacturable 3D DRAM (fact 2): staircase contacts and decoder area grow with tier count; this keeps periphery area nearly flat from 26 to 100+ tiers.

title: Array cell capacitors as flying caps for on-die converters
idea: Wire blocks of spare and edge DRAM cell capacitors (very high density at ~5 fF each) into a multi-phase switched-capacitor converter that generates VPP, VBB and VARY at ~80-85% efficiency instead of ~30-40% for Dickson charge pumps.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 10, 7): pumps take ~5% of die and waste power; doubling pump efficiency cuts wordline and refresh supply energy ~15-20%.

title: Coincident X-Y selection with dual-gate access transistor
idea: Like core memory's coincident-current selection, give each access transistor two gates (row wordline plus a column-segment select line) so only cells where both are high open; activating a cache line opens 64-512 cells, not an 8 kb row.
why: Overfetch (fact 8) and row hammer (fact 9): removes most of the 128x overfetch (~5.9 pJ to under 1 pJ per useful bit) and confines hammer exposure to a segment.

title: Old-node DRAM arrays bonded to 40nm periphery in CIS fabs
idea: Strip the periphery from 2x-nm DRAM array designs still running in depreciated lines, and hybrid-bond those wafers face-to-face to 40/28 nm logic periphery wafers using the wafer-to-wafer bonding lines that image-sensor fabs already run at volume; SAs connect through ~1-2 um pitch pads per bitline-pair group.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and capital (fact 4): ~1.6x bits per wafer from old DRAM lines with no new fab, using idle 28-40 nm logic and existing CIS bonding tools.

title: DIMM PMIC takes over VPP and VBB generation
idea: Extend the existing 180/130 nm BCD power-management chip on DDR5 modules with two more rails (VPP ~3 V and a negative VBB) delivered through dedicated balls, so DRAM dies delete their charge pumps and pump decap; inductor-based BCD converters run at ~90% versus ~30-40% for on-die pumps.
why: Periphery area (~5% of die) and energy (fact 10); trailing BCD capacity is plentiful.

title: Controller-held repair map replaces on-die fuse banks
idea: Write wafer-test repair results to the module SPD EEPROM; at boot the memory controller loads the bad-row/column map into its own address-translation table and steers accesses to spare rows exposed as ordinary addresses, so the DRAM die drops laser/e-fuse banks and redundancy-compare logic.
why: Periphery (fact 7): ~2-4% die area and ~0.5-1 ns of tRCD, and lets older lines ship dies with more defects (yield up).

title: Kerf-resident BIST and test modes sawn off after sort
idea: Place BIST engines, test-mode decoders and probe-only analog monitors in the scribe lanes, wired across the kerf to each die; they run at wafer sort and are physically discarded at dicing, leaving only a lockout fuse on the die.
why: Periphery (fact 7): test circuitry is ~3-5% of die area; reclaiming it gives ~3-5% more dies per wafer on existing lines at zero capex.

title: Inductive coil links replace TSVs in trailing-node stacks
idea: Stack 8 trailing-node DRAM dies with no TSVs: data and commands move vertically through on-chip coils drawn in existing top-metal layers (ThruChip-style inductive coupling), while power arrives through staircase wire bonds at OSATs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): avoids TSV processing and its ~20-30% yield loss, giving ~1 Tb/s stacked bandwidth from legacy fabs plus wire-bond capacity.

title: Predecoder XOR key rotates the row map each epoch
idea: Add a 16-bit XOR stage to the row predecoder whose key is re-randomized every refresh window, migrating data row by row during the refresh walk that already reads and restores every row, so an attacker's physical neighbors change unpredictably and hammer counts never accumulate on fixed victims.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): defeats targeted ~1k-activation attacks without large counter tables; a gates-only change any old node can build.

title: Leaky integrator capacitor counts activations in analog
idea: Fuse a charge-deposit circuit into each sub-wordline driver group: every ACT dumps a fixed charge packet onto a small capacitor that leaks with a ~64 ms time constant, and when its voltage crosses a comparator threshold the group's neighbor rows get refreshed. It is a row-hammer counter with no SRAM or digital logic.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): per-row-group tracking for under 1% area, versus large CAM/SRAM counter tables; works on any process.

title: Oscillator timed by real DRAM cells clocks refresh
idea: Build a relaxation oscillator whose timing element is a group of real array cells (same capacitor and access transistor) discharging to a threshold; its period tracks actual retention across temperature, voltage and process and directly sets each bank's refresh interval.
why: Refresh (fact 3): replaces the worst-case 64 ms plus temperature bins with tracked retention, typically 2-4x fewer refreshes for most dies and conditions.

title: Boot-calibrated dummy cells cancel each sense amp's offset
idea: At power-up, measure each SA's offset by sweeping a reference on a dummy bitline cell, then write a compensating charge into a per-bitline dummy cell that is charge-shared with the real cell on every read and refreshed with the row.
why: Sense margin (facts 1, 7): 3-4x lower effective offset allows 2x longer bitlines (half the SA stripes, ~8-10% die area) on existing processes.

title: Two bits per cell using old nodes' fat capacitors
idea: Trailing 2x-3x nm DRAM nodes have ~15-25 fF cells; pair that surplus charge with time-domain multilevel sensing, where a ramped reference and a counter in the SA stripe quantize four charge levels per cell.
why: Density and cost per bit (facts 1, 4): ~1.8x bits per wafer after ECC overhead, from fully depreciated old fabs with no new lithography.

title: Window-comparator sense amps flag uncertain bits as erasures
idea: Add a pair of offset-shifted comparators on the secondary sense path that flags bits whose sensed value fell inside a narrow uncertainty window; on-die ECC treats them as erasures, and erasure decoding corrects about 2x more bits than errors at unknown positions.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): tolerating ~2x more weak bits stretches refresh intervals ~2-4x using circuits old nodes already build.

title: Pair partial-good dies behind a 65nm bank-remap bridge
idea: Instead of scrapping or down-binning dies with dead banks, package two partial-good dies with a small 65 nm bridge chip that presents one standard full-capacity die and routes each bank address to whichever die has it working.
why: Usable supply: recovers ~5-10% of wafer output now scrapped or sold as low density, using only trailing logic and OSAT capacity.

title: Legacy DDR4 dies aggregated by a 28nm CXL base
idea: Co-package 8-16 dies from mature DDR4 lines on a 28 nm logic base that runs the DDR4 cores slowly but wide in parallel and exposes a CXL memory interface, taking over refresh management, ECC and hammer mitigation in the base.
why: Supply and capital (fact 4): turns trailing DDR4 capacity into a usable server memory tier at near-zero capex; base dies can be made in U.S. trailing fabs.

title: Registering clock driver stores weak-row map, targets refresh
idea: Load a per-row retention profile (from test or in-field scrubbing) into a small SRAM in the DIMM's registering clock driver, which is already a trailing-node chip; it lowers auto-refresh frequency and inserts targeted ACT/PRE refreshes only for the ~0.1% weak rows.
why: Refresh (fact 3): ~3-4x fewer refresh operations, reclaiming ~10% bandwidth and ~20% idle power on DDR5 modules without changing the DRAM die.

title: Bank-to-bank recycling of bitline restore charge
idea: When a bank precharges, its bitlines (half at VARY, half at ground) are not simply equalized to VBLP; a switch matrix first dumps the high-side charge into the reservoir feeding the next bank's restore, recycling about half the bitline charge.
why: Voltage floor and energy (fact 10): bitline swing dominates array energy; ~30-40% lower activation energy from a circuit-only change.

title: Software-switchable twin-cell mode per subarray
idea: Add a switch in each SA stripe so a subarray runs either as 1T1C (full capacity) or as 2T2C differential pairs (half capacity, ~4-8x retention and margin); the OS chooses the mode per subarray by workload and temperature.
why: Refresh and reliability (facts 3, 9): a flexible density-versus-retention trade lets marginal old-line dies ship and lets hot deployments skip most refresh.

title: Column-gated local wordline drivers activate one-eighth rows
idea: AND each sub-wordline driver enable with a column-segment signal decoded from the column address, so an ACT opens only the ~1 kb segment holding the requested data; the gate fits in existing SWD strips on old processes.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): ~5-8x lower activation energy per random access, and ~8x less hammer coupling per activate (fact 9).

title: Open array-periphery bond standard plus CHIPS grants
idea: Publish an open die-to-die standard that fixes the bitline-group, wordline and power pinout between DRAM array wafers and periphery wafers, and use CHIPS-style grants to have U.S. trailing logic fabs (90-22 nm) build the periphery tier for any array maker.
why: U.S. manufacturability (1-2% share): moves about half of each die's function into existing U.S. capacity without a new DRAM fab.

title: Bipolar-input sense amps on bonded SiGe BiCMOS die
idea: Bond array wafers to 130 nm SiGe BiCMOS periphery wafers, where bipolar input pairs (Vbe matching ~1 mV versus ~10-20 mV for small MOSFETs) sense bitlines through an 8:1 column mux, reading groups in rapid sequence.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): 5-10x lower offset allows ~3x smaller Cs or ~4x longer bitlines, using idle trailing BiCMOS fabs.

title: Display-fab panel interposers for wide-IO memory modules
idea: Use idle Gen-6 LCD lines (1.5-2 um lithography on large glass panels) to pattern multilayer redistribution interposers for wide, slow DRAM-to-processor links, replacing scarce silicon interposers.
why: Data movement (fact 5): wide-IO links at ~1 pJ/bit versus 10-20 pJ/bit for DDR5, and relief for the advanced-packaging bottleneck, using existing display capacity.

title: Bit-significance placement with per-subarray voltage and refresh
idea: Give each subarray its own VARY tap and refresh rate set by mode register; the memory controller places AI tensors' sign and exponent bits in strong, often-refreshed subarrays and low-order mantissa bits in low-voltage, rarely refreshed ones.
why: Refresh and voltage (facts 3, 10): ~40% lower array energy for weights and KV caches with negligible accuracy loss.

title: Charge-transfer presensing doubles cells per bitline
idea: Revive 1990s charge-transfer presensing: a Vt-compensated transfer transistor between a long bitline and a small sense node amplifies the signal by the capacitance ratio, so 1,024 cells per bitline work and the number of SA stripes halves.
why: Periphery (fact 7): SA stripes are ~20-25% of die; halving them saves ~10% die area on existing processes.

title: Bootstrapped wordline drivers revive 1980s self-boost, shrinking pumps
idea: Use per-driver-group MOS bootstrap capacitors to self-boost the wordline above VDD at activation, as early NMOS DRAMs did, so only a tiny VPP pump remains to hold leakage.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 10, 7): removes most charge-pump area and energy (~3-5% of die and a notable share of activation power).
